where: Section 3, bullet on Android and iOS
problem: "Android and iOS normally do not swap at all" is wrong for Android. Android does swap, but into a compressed region of RAM (zram), which the chapter itself calls "compressed RAM swap" in the Beyond section. The next sentence ("Android compresses some pages in RAM") contradicts the first, and a student could write in an exam that Android never swaps.
fix: "Android and iOS normally do not swap to disk. Android may swap into a compressed area of RAM (zram); iOS keeps no swap device. With no disk swap, both end idle background apps when memory runs short."

problem: "Swapping out a process that will be needed again within a few microseconds" uses a time scale that does not fit process scheduling; a student may read it literally as a hard cutoff.
fix: "Swapping out a process that will be needed again soon wastes disk bandwidth and delays it."

problem: The note "2.01 s for next process" silently assumes the incoming process is also 100 MB, the same size as the victim. The copy-in time depends on the incoming process's own size.
fix: Add the assumption to the caption or note: "2.01 s for a next process of 100 MB".

problem: "the rest of the time they reclaim pages and drop clean file pages" is muddled: reclaiming pages and dropping clean file pages are the same activity, and reclaiming may itself send pages to swap.
fix: "Unix-style systems keep a swap area and send pages to it only when free memory falls below a threshold; otherwise they free memory by dropping clean file pages and writing back dirty ones."
